title: Chapter 27 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: Stubb was the second mate. He came from Cape Cod, and so, by local custom, was called a Cape-Cod-man. He was happy-go-lucky, neither coward nor hero, meeting dangers as they came with an air of indifference; and in the tightest crisis of the chase he would keep working away, calm and collected, like a journeyman joiner hired by the year. Good-humored, relaxed, and carefree, he ran his whale-boat as if the deadliest encounter were just a dinner party and his crew all invited guests. He was as fussy about arranging his end of the boat comfortably as an old stagecoach driver is about how snug his seat is. When close up to the whale, in the very death-lock of the fight, he handled his merciless lance coolly and casually, the way a whistling tinker handles his hammer. He would hum his old rigadig tunes while side by side with the most furious monster. For this Stubb, long habit had turned the jaws of death into an easy chair. What he thought about death itself, nobody can say. Whether he ever thought about it at all might be a fair question; but if he ever did happen to turn his mind that way after a comfortable dinner, then no doubt, like a good sailor, he took it as a kind of call of the watch to tumble up aloft and get busy there with something he would find out about when he obeyed the order, and not before.

What, perhaps, along with other things, made Stubb such an easygoing, unfearing man, so cheerily trudging along with the burden of life in a world full of grave peddlers all bowed to the ground by their packs — what helped to bring about that almost impious good humor of his — that thing must have been his pipe. For, like his nose, his short, black little pipe was one of the regular features of his face. You would almost as soon have expected him to turn out of his bunk without his nose as without his pipe. He kept a whole row of pipes there, ready loaded, stuck in a rack within easy reach of his hand; and whenever he turned in, he smoked them all out one after another, lighting each from the last to the very end; then loaded them again to be ready once more. For when Stubb dressed, instead of first putting his legs into his trousers, he put his pipe into his mouth.

I say this constant smoking must have been one cause, at least, of his peculiar temperament. For everyone knows that the earthly air, whether on land or sea, is terribly infected with the nameless miseries of the countless people who have died breathing it. And just as during a cholera outbreak some people walk around pressing camphor-soaked handkerchiefs to their mouths, so too, against all mortal troubles, Stubb's tobacco smoke may have served as a kind of disinfectant.

The third mate was Flask, a native of Tisbury, on Martha's Vineyard. A short, stout, ruddy young fellow, very pugnacious about whales, who somehow seemed to think that the great leviathans had personally and hereditarily insulted him; and therefore it was a sort of point of honor with him to destroy them whenever he met them. So utterly lost was he to all sense of reverence for the many marvels of their majestic bulk and mystic ways, and so dead to anything like a sense of possible danger from encountering them, that in his poor opinion the wondrous whale was only a species of magnified mouse, or at least water rat, requiring only a little outmaneuvering and some small expense of time and trouble in order to kill and boil. This ignorant, unconscious fearlessness of his made him a little waggish on the subject of whales; he followed these fish for the fun of it; and a three-year voyage around Cape Horn was only a jolly joke that lasted that long. As a carpenter's nails are divided into wrought nails and cut nails, so mankind may be divided in the same way. Little Flask was one of the wrought ones, made to clinch tight and last long. They called him King-Post on board the Pequod, because in shape he could well be likened to the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers, which, by means of many radiating side timbers set into it, serves to brace the ship against the icy shocks of those battering seas.

Now these three mates — Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask — were important men. By universal tradition, they commanded three of the Pequod's boats as headsmen. In the grand battle formation in which Captain Ahab would likely arrange his forces to descend on the whales, these three headsmen were like company captains. Or, armed with their long, keen whaling lances, they were a chosen trio of lancers, just as the harpooners were throwers of javelins.

And since in this famous fishery each mate or headsman, like a Gothic knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooner, who at certain moments hands him a fresh lance when the first has been badly twisted or bent into an elbow in the attack; and since, moreover, a close intimacy and friendship generally exists between the two, it is only fitting that we set down here who the Pequod's harpooners were, and to which headsman each of them belonged.
First was Queequeg, whom Starbuck, the chief mate, had chosen as his squire. But Queequeg is already known to us.

Next was Tashtego, an unmixed Indian from Gay Head, the westernmost promontory of Martha's Vineyard, where there still exists the last remnant of a village of red men, which has long supplied the neighboring island of Nantucket with many of her most daring harpooners. In the fishery, they usually go by the general name of Gay Headers. Tashtego's long, lean, sable hair, his high cheekbones, and his black, rounded eyes — for an Indian, Oriental in their largeness, but Antarctic in their glittering expression — all this was enough to proclaim him an heir of the untainted blood of those proud warrior-hunters who, in quest of the great New England moose, had scoured the primeval forests of the mainland, bow in hand. But no longer sniffing the trail of the wild beasts of the woodland, Tashtego now hunted in the wake of the great whales of the sea, the unerring harpoon of the son fittingly replacing the infallible arrow of the fathers. Looking at the tawny brawn of his lithe, snaky limbs, you would almost have credited the superstitions of some of the earlier Puritans, and half-believed this wild Indian to be a son of the Prince of the Powers of the Air. Tashtego was the squire of Stubb, the second mate.

Third among the harpooners was Daggoo, a gigantic, coal-black negro-savage, with a lion-like tread — an Ahasuerus to behold. Hanging from his ears were two golden hoops, so large that the sailors called them ring-bolts, and would talk of securing the topsail halyards to them. In his youth Daggoo had voluntarily signed aboard a whaler lying in a lonely bay on his native coast. And having never been anywhere in the world but Africa, Nantucket, and the pagan harbors most visited by whalemen, and having now led for many years the bold life of the fishery in the ships of owners unusually careful about what sort of men they shipped, Daggoo kept all his barbaric virtues, and, erect as a giraffe, moved about the decks in all the pomp of six feet five in his socks. There was a bodily humility in looking up at him; and a white man standing before him seemed a white flag come to beg a truce of a fortress. Curious to say, this imperial negro, Ahasuerus Daggoo, was the squire of little Flask, who looked like a chess piece beside him. As for the rest of the Pequod's company, let it be said that at the present day not one in two of the many thousand men before the mast employed in the American whale fishery are American-born, though nearly all the officers are. In this the American whale fishery is the same as the American army and the military and merchant navies, and the engineering forces employed in building the American canals and railroads. The same, I say, because in all these cases the native American liberally provides the brains, and the rest of the world as generously supplies the muscles. No small number of these whaling seamen belong to the Azores, where the outward-bound Nantucket whalers often call to fill out their crews from the hardy peasants of those rocky shores. In the same way, the Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London put in at the Shetland Islands to take on their full complement of crew, and on the passage home they drop them there again. How it is, there is no telling, but islanders seem to make the best whalemen. They were nearly all islanders in the Pequod — Isolatoes too, as I call them, not acknowledging the common continent of men, but each Isolato living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, federated along one keel, what a set these Isolatoes were! An Anacharsis Clootz deputation from all the isles of the sea and all the ends of the earth, accompanying old Ahab in the Pequod to lay the world's grievances before that bar from which not very many of them ever come back. Black little Pip — he never did — oh, no! he went before. Poor Alabama boy! On the grim Pequod's forecastle you shall soon see him, beating his tambourine; a prelude to the eternal time when, sent for to the great quarter-deck on high, he was told to strike in with the angels and beat his tambourine in glory; called a coward here, hailed a hero there!
